hook_text: Astronomers pointed a telescope at the emptiest patch of sky they could find, for ten days. It was full of galaxies.
clip_script: In 1995, astronomers aimed the Hubble Space Telescope at a patch of sky smaller than a grain of sand held at arm's length. It looked completely empty. They collected its faint light for ten days. Almost every speck in the picture was a whole galaxy, about three thousand of them. Our Milky Way is one galaxy among hundreds of billions, maybe two trillion. They come as spirals like ours, smooth egg-shaped ellipticals, and shapeless irregulars like the Magellanic Clouds. They gather into families held by gravity. Ours is the Local Group. And the families are all moving apart, because space itself is stretching, like raisins in rising dough. Run it backward and everything began expanding about thirteen point eight billion years ago. Light has only had that long to reach us, so there is an edge to what we can see. Because space kept stretching, that edge is now forty-six billion light years away.
visual_style: A whiteboard hand holding a grain of sand against a black sky, zooming into a field of tiny galaxy sketches, then three galaxy shapes labelled, then raisin bread rising, then a circle labelled 'observable Universe' with a horizon line.
pacing: One famous image, then a cascade of scales out to the edge of what we can see.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find out why the edge is further than 13.8 billion light years.
